title: vws rescue wagon shifts into first gear 2026 09 04
author: Aimee Donnellan
text:
DUBLIN, Sept 4 (Reuters Breakingviews) - A union voting for a plan
, opens new tab
 that would see 100,000 redundancies speaks volumes about the existential crisis Europe’s car industry finds itself in. On Thursday night, Volkswagen’s (VOWG.DE)
, opens new tab
 supervisory board struck a turnaround ​plan which will cut the number of models it makes, shutter plants and rein in spending elsewhere. If it works, CEO Oliver Blume ‌will eventually be running a company with a healthy 9% operating margin. But very few things are within his control and the journey to his destination could be bumpy.
The fact that the deal came together at all seems to have surprised markets. VW’s shares had traded down most of the week as investors prepared for a delay or no deal at all, given the German group's supervisory ​board is stacked with labour representatives and public sector shareholders who have historically resisted change. But in the end, the board unanimously approved the proposal, ​which include cutting the number of models by half and an extra 50,000 job cuts on top of 50,000 agreed in 2024. ⁠That may be because, with Chinese rivals like BYD (002594.SZ)
, opens new tab
, (1211.HK)
, opens new tab
 flooding the European market with cheaper and more tech-laden cars, such harsh measures are becoming unavoidable.
The “how” is where Blume ​may run into trouble. Despite pledging to slash jobs, Blume has not yet given much detail on how he will reach the 9% operating margin by 2030. Last year, ​the business only managed 2.8% and is forecast to reach 6.4% by 2030, per Visible Alpha forecasts. And his numbers rely on the assumption that VW will be able to keep selling the same nine million vehicles every year. That may be hard given Chinese automakers doubled their share of new European car sales to 15% in the first six months of the year.
And much of the ​pain has been put off. VW has promised no mandatory redundancies until 2030. It has not even agreed to shut its least efficient German plants, but simply said ​it cannot yet commit to using them beyond 2031. Nor has it said how much it will cost to shut those factories. That may be why Blume has committed to selling more ‌assets. VW’s ⁠over 85% stake in €19 billion commercial vehicle group Traton (8TRA.DE)
, opens new tab
 is an obvious place to start. Blume may prefer to safeguard his 75% stake in €40 billion Porsche (P911_p.DE)
, opens new tab
 as well as Lamborghini given they are relatively sheltered from Chinese carmakers' advance, but he may have little choice but to sell, or trim, those crown jewels to help pay for necessary changes.
Blume seems to be gearing up for bigger actions. Part of Thursday’s announcement is a plan to streamline the German group’s governance to reduce the number of decisions that ​require sign off from the supervisory board. ​This could make it easier for ⁠Volkswagen management to push through cuts, or cull more models than the 50% he has already earmarked.
For now, investors are not giving Blume much credit. The news saw the German group's shares jump 5% on Friday. But the company is still at trading at ​less than 4 times forward earnings. That may be because the plan will take time to deliver. The bigger issue ​is that no matter ⁠what Blume does, he will need EU lawmakers to be willing to risk a trade war with China to stop more cheap imports flooding the market. The good news, however, is that Volkswagen's turnaround is finally shifting into first gear.
(Corrects Porsche stock symbol in paragraph four.)
